agent_returns.text:
The tool confirms the year difference perfectly: 14 February 1746 Old Style = 14 February 1747 New Style. The offset is exactly 1 year, which is the standard Old Style / New Style year-start adjustment for any date falling between 1 January and 24 March in pre-1752 England. Per the rules here, when the competing dates differ by exactly what the tool returns, **this is not a substantive conflict — do not create a conflict entry.**

Here is what happened. England's civil year began on 25 March (Lady Day) until the Calendar Act took effect in September 1752. A February date therefore fell at the tail end of the old year. The curate who made the register entry wrote "1746" because in his reckoning the new year had not yet turned; that is the date as actually recorded on the page. When the Parish Register Society transcriber prepared the printed edition — after 1752, when England had already switched to a 1 January year-start — the transcriber silently modernized the year to 1747. Neither figure is wrong; each is correct under the convention its writer was using.

**What to record.** The register's own hand (a_001, 14 February 1746 OS) is the original, contemporary, authoritative source. The transcript (a_002) is a derivative of the same entry and, for this fact, carries no independent weight. The scholarly convention for a date in this ambiguous window is to use a double-dated year: **14 February 1746/7**, which makes the OS/NS distinction explicit for any reader. Record that form as the baptism date, cite the original register as the source, and add a brief note that the transcript's "1747" is the same date modernized to the New Style year.

No conflict entry is needed in this project, and no further research step is required to settle the year question.

---

The two records turn out to describe the same baptism day written under two different year-counting conventions: the original parish register used the old English reckoning (new year on 25 March), giving February as still in 1746, while the later printed transcript silently updated it to the modern reckoning (new year on 1 January), giving 1747. The scholarly way to record this is as a double-dated year — 14 February 1746/7 — which shows both conventions at once and flags the ambiguity for future researchers.

No further step is needed; the register entry is the authoritative source, and the transcript adds nothing new for this date.
